title: Dumplings have giants, buns don't: machines can't replicate the hand-pinch feel
dek: Dumplings and glutinous rice balls were scaled by giants like Sifu and Sanquan, but buns require fermented dough and hand-pinched pleats—machines can't achieve that fluffiness—so for a decade, the category has left room for smaller brands.
why: It explains a counterintuitive fact: a company that focused only on buns for ten years outpaced capital-backed competitors by relying on a handmade barrier machines cannot replicate.
who: For consumer-brand founders and investors tracking traditional food categories, curious why buns lack giants, and wanting to understand slow-growth strategies.
skip: Around 51:57, discussion of burgers, lamb skewers, and other industry gossip—low information value, can skip.

points.h: Regional dominance becomes a liability when scaling to national competition
points.body: The brand built strong word-of-mouth in Shanghai's refrigerated-food market, but when it tried to scale nationally with frozen products, it crashed. Consumers had never heard of the brand and only compared prices; the products felt too sweet, not fluffy enough, not firm enough for national tastes. The supply-chain advantage formed regionally evaporated instantly when competing in the uniform, price-driven national frozen-food category.

points.h: Visible filling became the breakthrough product that drove growth
points.body: After the national setback, the team stopped trying to recreate classic flavors and made their first genuinely differentiated product: cheese-filled buns with the filling placed on the outside, visible at a glance. This product launched at the moment when Xiaohongshu users wanted ‘see what you get’, and visibility and novelty created organic word-of-mouth. It was the team's first real success after stepping out of their comfort zone.

points.h: A hit product spreads in weeks but the original survives when imitations fade
points.body: The cheese-filled bun took nine months to develop and optimize, but competitors could replicate it in roughly a month. After the product went viral, over a dozen cheaper knockoffs flooded the market in two years. The team panicked enough to consider switching to cheaper mechanization and lower-cost ingredients, but nothing reproduced the same texture. Eventually, time proved the principle: the imitations disappeared, and consumers kept buying the original.

points.h: Dead dough scales to giants; live dough stays artisanal because machines can't pinch
points.body: Dumplings and glutinous rice balls use unleavened dough that needs no fermentation and was mechanized from the start, which is why Sifu and Sanquan became giants and essentially closed off the space for newcomers. Buns use leavened dough that must ferment and be hand-pinched into a dozen pleats—when a machine does it, the fluffiness that skilled hands create is gone. This is why the bun category has stayed regional and handmade, paradoxically leaving room for new brands.

points.h: Even in tier-three cities, consumers will pay extra for quality
points.body: While attending Pang Donglai's central kitchen during the height of 9.99-yuan price wars, the sourcing and production standards were remarkably high and the product wasn't cheap, yet consumers still bought in. People in that tier-three city seemed more relaxed and happy than in tier-one cities. This convinced him that the premium for health-conscious choices was sustainable. He returned and told the team not to panic: quality products will be recognized.

points.h: Bootstrapping stays steady when venture money makes boom-and-bust cycles
points.body: The company has never raised capital. Manufacturing heritage made the team extremely cautious about spending; development has been steady but slow. The e-commerce business is still in investment mode, not profitable. Peers who raised and spent aggressively hit ten-billion-yuan scale, then crashed back down to one or two billion. The founder believes in compounding slowly through repeat purchases rather than chasing growth that evaporates when marketing stops.

points.h: Categories sealed by unit economics and scale should be avoided entirely
points.body: The company deliberately skips dumplings and wontons because those are crushed by scale effects and procurement costs—even with the best supply chain, you'd likely get flattened anyway. It also abandoned baked goods because specialized factories already own the baking equipment and supply chains needed to compete. The team decided it can only build a moat in fermented and leavened pastries, where handwork is hard to mechanize.

points.h: Better doesn't win when the product photographs worse
points.body: The team developed white-filling pork buns, believing them more authentic and closer to the original pork taste than the red-filled versions dominating the market. Pricing was not higher, yet consumers showed complete indifference. The root cause, on review, partly traces to white filling looking poor on video for e-commerce—yet small soup dumplings with white filling remain perennial bestsellers. That contradiction, they say, remains unsolved.

quotes.text: We were always very confident—thought our products tasted great, had excellent consumer word-of-mouth, sold very well in Shanghai. Didn't we think that once we set prices competitively, everyone would flock to carry us? But actually, we suffered a major blow.

It's a paradox—it's a paradox—but what's fascinating is that several of our products go through the same experience: after launch, once they hit big, the market gets flooded with them, they're everywhere—but as time passes, a year or two later, they all disappear. Consumers still buy ours. So this journey of emergence and fade is quite fascinating.

I think the world follows natural law: there's an ecological principle that the stronger the resistance and stability, the weaker the recovery and resilience. A rainforest can withstand almost anything, but once it's destroyed, it's hard to recover.
And building a brand—actually, when I left Xiaonanoguo, everyone had this: everyone has a brand dream, right? I think people can understand that.
So I'm thinking: this is what life is about. If this is the right path, then everyone should spend a little extra money for our health and eating, and what we get in return is a happy life.
We come from manufacturing, always very conservative on spending—I think everyone understands that—so our development has been quite steady.

We spent a lot of time researching the white-filled pork bun. After launch, consumers seemed completely indifferent, but we were thrilled. We thought it was truly innovative, completely different from what's on the market—everyone has red filling, only we have white.
